content: Cerebral malaria is a condition that involves swelling of the brain. Corticosteroid drugs have the potential to reduce the harmful effects of this brain swelling. However, these drugs may also suppress the immune system's ability to fight the infection. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of corticosteroid drugs in patients with cerebral malaria, specifically focusing on outcomes such as death, life-threatening complications, and any residual disabilities in survivors. A comprehensive search for relevant studies was conducted in March 2008. The databases searched included the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL (The Cochrane Library 2008, Issue 1), MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and mRCT. Additionally, reference lists of relevant studies were reviewed. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized controlled trials that compared the use of corticosteroids to no corticosteroids, with all other treatments being identical, in patients diagnosed with cerebral malaria. Two independent authors assessed the eligibility of the trials, evaluated the risk of bias (methodological quality), and extracted data. The outcomes of interest included death, death associated with life-threatening complications, other clinical complications, and disability. Two trials, involving a total of 143 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Across these trials, there were 30 deaths, with an even distribution between the corticosteroid and control groups. The calculated risk ratio for death was 0.89, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 0.48 to 1.68, based on the 143 participants. Clinical complications were reported as the number of events in each trial group. However, these reports did not exclude complications that occurred in patients who died. This made it challenging to interpret the data, particularly as there were significantly more episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding and seizures in the corticosteroid group. Neither of the two trials assessed disability as an outcome. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence to suggest a benefit from corticosteroid use in cerebral malaria. However, the small number of participants in the trials makes it difficult to definitively rule out an effect on mortality in either direction. Additionally, the data on clinical complications are challenging to interpret due to the limitations in reporting.
